current_episode.title: Episode 580: Plastic Surgery, Comparison, and the Hidden Cost of Chasing Perfection

guest.bio_context: Shani Suissa appears as a recurring co-host on the solo episodes of Habits and Hustle, described by host Jen as her 'friend and foil.' She personally underwent a rhinoplasty, septoplasty, and turbinate reduction approximately two years prior to this episode, and speaks from direct experience about the complications that followed, including a septum perforation requiring corrective surgery. She also had her hair colored by someone who underwent a lower facelift, giving her a close-range perspective on surgical outcomes.

context.real_quote: If you are pretty before, you're going to be pretty after. If you're ugly before, you're going to be uglier with a tighter face after. It's not going to change what you are.
key_stats: Rhinoplasty recovery: Shani Suissa still had visible swelling 2 years after her nose surgery, confirmed by her dermatologist during a laser facial appointment
Lower facelift cost: $24,000 for an off-social-media surgeon who performed what the hosts describe as an exceptional lower facelift on a 68-year-old hairdresser
High-end facelift cost: up to $250,000–$500,000 for celebrity-tier or social-media-famous plastic surgeons, compared to $24,000 for a non-social-media equivalent
Price inflation example: a procedure that once cost $8,000 now costs $20,000 due to the surge in popularity of cosmetic surgery
Social media surgeon premium: doctors active on social media charge 10 to 20 times more than off-social practitioners for comparable procedures, according to the hosts

pending_qa.q: How long does recovery from rhinoplasty actually take, and what is the real downtime?
pending_qa.r: Shani Suissa reports still being swollen two years after her rhinoplasty, a fact confirmed by her dermatologist during a laser facial visit. She notes that people vastly underestimate recovery time, and that the common advice to 'just get your nose done' treats a serious surgical procedure as casually as getting a Starbucks latte, which she strongly disputes.

pending_qa.q: Is a surgeon's social media popularity a reliable indicator of their surgical quality?
pending_qa.r: Shani Suissa and host Jen argue that a plastic surgeon who is very active on social media is likely spending more time creating content than performing surgeries, which they consider a major red flag. They point to the example of a hairdresser who got an excellent lower facelift for $24,000 from a surgeon who has no social media presence and is simply too busy with high-quality work to need one.

pending_qa.q: Does plastic surgery actually resolve personal insecurities, or do people simply shift focus to new ones?
pending_qa.r: Shani Suissa states that insecurities that exist before a cosmetic procedure will still exist after it, and that patients often simply move their fixation to a different body part. She uses her own rhinoplasty as an example, noting that she sometimes still nitpicks her nose even after the surgery, and that the host draws a parallel to people who lose weight and then immediately fixate on loose skin they never noticed before.

pending_qa.q: Why has plastic surgery become so much more accessible and normalized in recent years?
pending_qa.r: The hosts point to multiple converging factors: the rise of Zoom during and after COVID forcing people to stare at their own faces constantly, social media filters like Snapchat and face apps prompting people to bring AI-filtered images to surgeons as reference points, and the explosion of med spas appearing 'like Starbucks' on every city corner. These factors together have dramatically lowered the psychological barrier to seeking cosmetic procedures.

pending_qa.q: What is the trend of celebrities going 'au naturel' as plastic surgery becomes more accessible to the general public?
pending_qa.r: A recent headline noted that as plastic surgery becomes increasingly accessible to lower-income demographics, celebrities are reversing course and returning to a more natural look — no heavy surgery, minimal or very natural-looking makeup. The hosts observe that achieving a truly 'natural-looking' result now costs significantly more than generic procedures, effectively pricing the refined aesthetic back out of reach for most people and re-establishing class separation.

pending_qa.q: How should someone choose a plastic surgeon, and what financial cautions should they keep in mind?
pending_qa.r: Shani Suissa advises never choosing a surgeon based on cost savings, never 'cheaping out,' and waiting until you can afford a genuinely skilled practitioner rather than the cheapest option. She also recommends ensuring the surgeon has both the aesthetic vision aligned with what you want and a thorough understanding of the internal functional anatomy involved, as inadequate knowledge of the latter led directly to her own septum perforation.

pending_qa.q: Who is Dr. Jason Hamilton and what is he known for in rhinoplasty?
pending_qa.r: Shani Suissa recommends Dr. Jason Hamilton as a leading specialist for anyone seeking nose surgery, particularly for septum-related issues. She notes that very few doctors are willing or able to repair a septum perforation, positioning Hamilton as a rare expert in that specific sub-field of rhinoplasty.

pending_qa.q: How do social media filters and constant video exposure psychologically affect how people perceive their own appearance?
pending_qa.r: The hosts argue that humans were not biologically built to see their own reflections or outer appearance constantly, and that cameras, mirrors, and now video calls are modern inventions that have 'honestly really degraded our own personal self-love.' They suggest that people born in the 1800s, without constant photographic exposure to their own faces, would largely consider themselves quite attractive and would not be driven to seek surgical alteration.
